topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES
STRUCTURE
FIRST TERM
WEEK 1
PRIMARY 2
THEME - LISTENING AND SPEAKING
TOPIC - CONTENT COLUMN
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. read a simple passage on the content column.
2. write the passage in their notebook.
3. write clearly and observe the spacing between the letters in a word and words in a sentence.
ENTRY BEHAVIOURS
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Passage under content column.
2. Any other relevant reference materials.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
Course Book
All Relevant Material
Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
FOCUS READING:
A simple and short passage selected from the course book based on regard and concern for interest of others.
TOPIC - NATION VALUES (DISCIPLINE)
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Reads the passage with expression and correct intonation.
Pupil’s Activities - Listen the passage carefully.
3. Lets the pupils the passage in groups or pairs depending on the size of the class.
4. Allows the pupils to read individual.
Pupil’s Activities - Participate actively in the reading.
5. Guides pupils to identify the difficult words in the passage and observe the spacing between a word and words in a sentence.
Pupil’s Activities - Identify the difficult words in the passage and observe the spacing between a word and words in a sentence.
6. Asks pupils to copy the passage in their notebook.
Pupil’s Activities - Write as instructed.
7. Summarize the lesson.
Pupil’s Activities - Participate actively in lesson summary.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
LESSON EVALUATION
Ask pupils to:
1. read a simple passage on the content column.
2. write the passage in their notebook.
3. write clearly and observe the spacing between the letters in a word and words in a sentence.

topics.title: Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sound /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 1 English Phonics
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (PHONICS)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 1
THEME - PHONEMIC AWARENESS
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - AURAL DISCRIMINATION OF THE SOUND /ɜ/ AND /ʌ/
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction to phonemic awareness
2. Identification of the sounds /ɜ/ and /ʌ/
3. Words containing /ɜ/ and /ʌ/
4. Pronunciation and aural discrimination practice
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the simple meaning of phonemic awareness.
2. Identify the sounds /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ when they hear them.
3. Pronounce /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ correctly.
4. Identify words containing the /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ sound.
5. Distinguish between /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ when listening.
5. Use words containing the sounds in simple sentences.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can identify and pronounce common vowel sounds and read simple words.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Word cards, Picture cards, Sound cards, Flashcards
2. Pronunciation chart
3. Writing board
4. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses listening, demonstration, repetition, pronunciation drills, questioning, word identification, comparison, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by saying familiar words containing the two sounds and asks pupils to listen carefully.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Phonics charts
5. Dictionary
6. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Phonemic awareness is the ability to hear and identify individual sounds in spoken words.
Today, pupils will learn to listen for and distinguish between the sounds /ɜ/ and /ʌ/.
The sounds are different.
Examples of words containing /ɜ/ include: bird, girl, shirt, nurse, turn
Examples of words containing /ʌ/ include: cup, sun, bus, hut, duck
THE SOUND /ɜ/
The sound /ɜ/ is heard in words such as:
- bird
- girl
- shirt
- nurse
- turn
- word
- work
- first
- third
- learn
Pupils listen carefully and repeat the words.
THE SOUND /ʌ/
The sound /ʌ/ is heard in words such as:
- cup
- sun
- bus
- hut
- duck
- run
- fun
- cut
- jump
- lunch
Pupils listen carefully and repeat the words.
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN /ɜ/ AND /ʌ/
The two sounds are different.
/ɜ/: bird, girl, shirt, nurse, turn, word, work, first, third, learn
/ʌ/: cup, sun, bus, hut, duck, run, fun, cut, jump, lunch
The teacher says the words clearly. Pupils listen and identify the sound they hear.
AURAL DISCRIMINATION
Aural discrimination means listening carefully and telling the difference between sounds.
The teacher says one word at a time.
Pupils listen and say whether they hear /ɜ/ or /ʌ/.
Examples:
- bird - /ɜ/
- cup - /ʌ/
- girl - /ɜ/
- sun - /ʌ/
- shirt - /ɜ/
- bus - /ʌ/
- nurse - /ɜ/
- duck - /ʌ/
- turn - /ɜ/
- run - /ʌ/
LISTENING PRACTICE
The teacher says pairs of words.
Pupils listen and identify whether the sounds are the same or different.
Examples:
- bird - bus → Different
- cup - sun → Same
- girl - shirt → Same
- nurse - duck → Different
- turn - run → Different
- work - word → Same
The teacher repeats the activity with other familiar words.
PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE
The teacher models each sound clearly.
- /ɜ/: bird, girl, shirt, nurse, turn
- /ʌ/: cup, sun, bus, hut, duck
Pupils repeat the words individually and together.
The teacher corrects pronunciation where necessary.
SENTENCES WITH THE WORDS
1. The bird is in the tree.
2. The girl has a bag.
3. My shirt is clean.
4. The nurse is kind.
5. Please turn around.
6. I have a cup.
7. The sun is hot.
8. The bus is coming.
9. The duck can swim.
10. I can run fast.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Which sound is heard in the word “bird”? A. /ʌ/ B. /ɜ/ C. /æ/
2. Which word contains the /ʌ/ sound? A. Shirt B. Nurse C. Cup
3. Which word contains the /ɜ/ sound? A. Girl B. Bus C. Duck
4. Which sound is heard in “sun”? A. /ɜ/ B. /ʌ/ C. /iː/
5. Which pair contains words with the /ɜ/ sound?
A. bird and shirt
B. cup and bus
C. sun and duck
6. Which pair contains words with the /ʌ/ sound?
A. girl and nurse
B. cup and bus
C. bird and turn
7. Which word has a different vowel sound from “bird”? A. girl B. shirt C. bus
8. Which word has the same vowel sound as “cup”? A. sun B. nurse C. shirt
9. Which sound is heard in “nurse”? A. /ʌ/ B. /ɜ/ C. /æ/
10. What should pupils do to distinguish between /ɜ/ and /ʌ/?
A. Read without listening
B. Ignore the sounds
C. Listen carefully to the sounds
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. C 3. A 4. B 5. A
6. B. 7. C 8. A 9. B 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that phonemic awareness involves hearing and identifying individual sounds in spoken words.
They learned to identify and distinguish between the sounds /ɜ/ and /ʌ/. They practised listening to words such as bird, girl, shirt, nurse, turn, cup, sun, bus, hut and duck.
Pupils also practised grouping words according to their vowel sounds and using some of the words in simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher says familiar words such as bird, cup, girl and bus and asks pupils to listen carefully to the vowel sounds.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen to the words and identify the sounds they hear.
Step 2: Introducing the Sound /ɜ/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces the sound /ɜ/ and pronounces words such as bird, girl, shirt, nurse and turn.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the sound and the words.
Step 3: Introducing the Sound /ʌ/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces the sound /ʌ/ and pronounces words such as cup, sun, bus, hut and duck.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the sound and the words.
Step 4: Comparing the Sounds
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ are different vowel sounds and gives examples of words containing each sound.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen to pairs of words and identify whether the sounds are the same or different.
Step 5: Aural Discrimination Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher says words one at a time and asks pupils to identify whether each word contains /ɜ/ or /ʌ/.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify the sound they hear.
Step 6: Pronunciation Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher pronounces words containing /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ and guides pupils to repeat them correctly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words individually and in groups.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five words containing /ɜ/.
- Group 2: Identify five words containing /ʌ/.
- Group 3: Sort word cards into /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ groups.
- Group 4: Read five words aloud and identify their vowel sounds.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, sort, pronounce and present words according to their vowel sounds.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the sounds /ɜ/ and /ʌ/, their examples and how to distinguish them by listening. The teacher gives pupils the 10 assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and pronounce selected words containing the two sounds.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to listen carefully to spoken words, identify vowel sounds and practise pronouncing /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ correctly.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is phonemic awareness?
2. What sound is heard in “bird”?
3. What sound is heard in “cup”?
4. Mention three words containing /ɜ/.
5. Mention three words containing /ʌ/.

topics.title: Stories built on Road Safety Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 1 English Structure
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (STRUCTURE)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 1
THEME - STRUCTURE
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - STORY BUILT ON ROAD SAFETY
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction to road safety
2. Reading a simple road-safety story
3. Identifying sentences in the story
4. Constructing simple sentences
5. Guided and group practice
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the simple meaning of road safety.
2. Read a short story about road safety.
3. Identify simple sentences in the story.
4. Identify nouns and verbs used in the story.
5. Mention common road-safety words.
6. Use road-safety words in simple sentences.
7. Construct simple sentences correctly.
8. State simple road-safety rules.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can read simple sentences and identify common nouns and verbs.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Road-safety picture cards
2. Word cards, Flashcards
3. Traffic-light chart
4. Road-safety signs
5. Writing board
6. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses reading aloud, explanation, questioning, demonstration, repetition, sentence construction, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by showing pupils pictures of a road, traffic light and pedestrians and asks them to talk about what they see.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Road-safety charts
5. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Road safety means using the road carefully and following rules that help to prevent accidents.
People should be careful when walking, crossing the road or travelling in a vehicle.
STORY: KOLA AND THE SAFE ROAD
Kola was going to school with his sister.
They came to a busy road. Kola wanted to cross quickly.
His sister said, “Stop and look before crossing.”
They stopped at the roadside and looked left and right.
The traffic light was red, so they waited.
When it was safe to cross, they walked carefully across the road.
Kola was happy because they crossed the road safely.
He learned that we must always obey road-safety rules.
UNDERSTANDING THE STORY
The story teaches pupils to:
- stop before crossing a busy road;
- look left and right;
- obey traffic lights;
- cross when it is safe; and
- follow road-safety rules.
NEW WORDS AND MEANINGS
1. Road - a place where vehicles and people move.
2. Safety - being protected from danger.
3. Cross - to move from one side to another.
4. Traffic light - a light that controls road traffic.
5. Red - the traffic-light colour that tells road users to stop.
6. Wait - to stay until it is safe or the right time.
7. Busy - having many people or vehicles.
8. Carefully - doing something with care.
SENTENCES FROM THE STORY
1. Kola was going to school.
2. They came to a busy road.
3. Kola wanted to cross quickly.
4. They stopped at the roadside.
5. They looked left and right.
6. The traffic light was red.
7. They waited.
8. They walked carefully across the road.
NOUNS IN THE STORY
A noun is a name of a person, place, animal or thing.
Examples from the story: Kola, sister, school, road, roadside, traffic light
VERBS IN THE STORY
A verb is a word that shows an action.
Examples from the story: going, came, wanted, cross, stop, look, waited, walked, learned
MAKING SIMPLE SENTENCES
Pupils can use road-safety words to make simple sentences.
Examples:
- I cross the road carefully.
- We obey road rules.
- The traffic light is red.
- I wait before crossing.
- We look left and right.
- The road is busy.
- Kola walks to school.
- We follow safety rules.
ROAD-SAFETY RULES
Pupils should:
1. Stop before crossing a busy road.
2. Look left and right before crossing.
3. Obey traffic lights.
4. Cross at a safe place.
5. Walk carefully on the road.
6. Avoid playing on the road.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is road safety?
A. Playing on the road
B. Using the road carefully and following safety rules
C. Running across the road
2. Who was going to school?
A. Kola
B. Musa
C. Tunde
3. What did Kola and his sister come to?
A. A farm
B. A busy road
C. A playground
4. What did Kola’s sister tell him to do?
A. Run quickly
B. Stop and look before crossing
C. Play on the road
5. What colour was the traffic light?
A. Green
B. Yellow
C. Red
6. What did they do when the light was red?
A. They waited.
B. They ran.
C. They played.
7. Which word is a noun?
A. Cross
B. Road
C. Walk
8. Which word is a verb?
A. School
B. Road
C. Walk
9. Which sentence is correctly written?
A. We obey road rules.
B. we obey road rules
C. We obey road rules
10. What should pupils do before crossing the road?
A. Play
B. Stop and look carefully
C. Run without looking
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. A 3. B 4. B 5. C
6. A 7. B 8. C 9. A 10. B
SUMMARY
Pupils read a simple story about Kola and his sister and learned important road-safety rules.
They learned how to identify nouns and verbs in the story and how to use road-safety words to make simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pictures of a road, traffic light and pedestrians and asks pupils what they can see.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and talk about what they see.
Step 2: Reading the Story
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher displays the story “Kola and the Safe Road” and reads it aloud clearly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and read the story after the teacher.
Step 3: Understanding the Story
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks simple questions about what happened in the story and explains the road-safety rules.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention road-safety rules.
Step 4: Identifying Nouns
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains nouns and asks pupils to identify nouns such as Kola, school, road and traffic light.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and read the nouns aloud.
Step 5: Identifying Verbs
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains verbs and asks pupils to identify action words such as walk, cross, stop and wait.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and use the verbs in simple sentences.
Step 6: Making Simple Sentences
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates how to make simple sentences using road-safety words.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils make and read simple sentences about road safety.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five nouns from the story.
- Group 2: Identify five verbs from the story.
- Group 3: Make five simple sentences using road-safety words.
- Group 4: State five road-safety rules.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, construct, discuss and present their answers.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the story, nouns, verbs, simple sentences and road-safety rules. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and make simple sentences about road safety.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to obey road-safety rules, use simple sentences correctly and always be careful when using the road.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is road safety?
2. Mention three road-safety rules.
3. Mention two nouns from the story.
4. Mention two verbs from the story.
5. Make one sentence about road safety.

topics.title: Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sounds /ɔ/ and /ɔ:/ Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 2 English Phonics
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (PHONICS)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 2
THEME - PHONEMIC AWARENESS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sounds /ɜ/ and /ʌ/ Primary 3 (Basic 3) Week 1 English Phonics
TOPIC - AURAL DISCRIMINATION OF THE SOUNDS /ɔ/ AND /ɔ:/
LEARNING AREA
1. Meaning of phonemic awareness
2. Identification of the sounds /ɔ/ and /ɔː/
3. Words containing /ɔ/ and /ɔː/
4. Aural discrimination of the two sounds and Comparison of the sounds using word pairs
5. Pronunciation and listening practice
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain phonemic awareness.
2. Identify the sounds /ɔ/ and /ɔː/ when they hear them.
3. Pronounce words containing the two sounds.
4. Distinguish between /ɔ/ and /ɔː/ by listening.
5. Identify words containing /ɔ/.
6. Identify words containing /ɔː/.
7. Match words with similar but different vowel sounds.
8. Use selected words in simple sentences.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can listen to and identify common vowel sounds in simple words.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
1. Word cards, Picture cards, Sound cards, Flashcards
2. Phonics chart
3. Writing board
4. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses listening, demonstration, repetition, pronunciation drills, questioning, word identification, comparison, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by saying familiar words containing the two sounds and asks pupils to listen carefully.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Phonics chart
5. Dictionary
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Phonemic awareness is the ability to hear and identify individual sounds in spoken words.
Today, pupils will learn to listen carefully and distinguish between the sounds /ɔ/ and /ɔː/.
The sounds are similar, but they are different. Listening carefully helps us identify the difference.
THE SOUND /ɔ/
The sound /ɔ/ is heard in words such as:
- cot
- spot
- pot
- hot
- not
- shot
- lot
- dot
Pupils listen to the teacher and repeat each word.
THE SOUND /ɔː/
The sound /ɔː/ is heard in words such as:
- court
- sport
- port
- short
- bought
- caught
- taught
- fought
Pupils listen to the teacher and repeat each word.
CONTRASTING WORD PAIRS
The following pairs help pupils hear the difference between /ɔ/ and /ɔː/:
/ɔ/: cot, spot, pot, hot, not, shot, lot, dot
/ɔː/: court, sport, port, short, bought, caught, taught, fought
The teacher pronounces each pair clearly. Pupils listen carefully and repeat.
AURAL DISCRIMINATION
Aural discrimination means listening carefully and identifying differences between sounds.
The teacher says one word at a time. Pupils listen and identify whether they hear /ɔ/ or /ɔː/.
Examples:
- cot - /ɔ/
- court - /ɔː/
- spot - /ɔ/
- sport - /ɔː/
- pot - /ɔ/
- port - /ɔː/
- hot - /ɔ/
- short - /ɔː/
LISTENING PRACTICE
The teacher says pairs of words. Pupils listen and say whether the vowel sounds are the same or different.
- cot - court → Different
- spot - sport → Different
- pot - port → Different
- hot - short → Different
- cot - spot → Same
- court - sport → Same
- pot - hot → Same
- port - short → Same
PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE
The teacher models the words clearly.
- /ɔ/: cot, spot, pot, hot, not
- /ɔː/: court, sport, port, short, caught
Pupils repeat the words individually and together.
SIMPLE SENTENCES
1. The baby sleeps in a cot.
2. There is a spot on my shirt.
3. The soup is in the pot.
4. The food is hot.
5. I am not late.
6. The case was taken to court.
7. We enjoy sport.
8. The ship is in the port.
9. My brother is short.
10. She caught the ball.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Which sound is heard in “cot”? A. /ɔ:/ B. /ɔ/ C. /ʌ/
2. Which word contains the /ɔː/ sound? A. Sport B. Spot C. Pot
3. Which word contains the /ɔ/ sound? A. Court B. Port C. Cot
4. Which pair has different vowel sounds?
A. cot - court
B. spot - cot
C. court - sport
5. Which word contains the /ɔː/ sound? A. Hot B. Port C. Dot
6. Which word contains the /ɔ/ sound? A. Short B. Caught C. Spot
7. Which pair has the same vowel sound?
A. pot - hot
B. pot - port
C. cot - court
8. Which pair has different vowel sounds?
A. court - sport
B. pot - port
C. spot - hot
9. Which word contains the /ɔː/ sound? A. Not B. Lot C. Sport
10. What should pupils do to distinguish between /ɔ/ and /ɔː/?
A. Ignore the sounds
B. Listen carefully to the sounds
C. Guess the words
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. A 3. C 4. A 5. B
6. C 7. A 8. B 9. C 10. B
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that phonemic awareness means listening to and identifying individual sounds in spoken words.
They learned to distinguish between /ɔ/ and /ɔː/ by listening to contrasting word pairs such as cot-court, spot-sport, pot-port and hot-short.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher revises the previous lesson and says some familiar words for pupils to listen to.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify the sounds they hear.
Step 2: Introducing /ɔ/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces /ɔ/ and pronounces words such as cot, spot, pot, hot and not.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the words.
Step 3: Introducing /ɔː/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces /ɔː/ and pronounces words such as court, sport, port, short and caught.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the words.
Step 4: Comparing the Sounds
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher presents contrasting pairs such as cot-court, spot-sport and pot-port and pronounces them clearly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and identify whether the vowel sounds are the same or different.
Step 5: Aural Discrimination Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher says individual words and asks pupils to identify whether they contain /ɔ/ or /ɔː/.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and identify the sound they hear.
Step 6: Pronunciation Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher pronounces contrasting words and guides pupils to repeat them correctly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words individually and in groups.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five words containing /ɔ/.
- Group 2: Identify five words containing /ɔː/.
- Group 3: Match contrasting pairs such as cot-court and spot-sport.
- Group 4: Read selected words aloud and identify their vowel sounds.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, match, pronounce and present the words.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the sounds /ɔ/ and /ɔː/ and the contrasting word pairs. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and pronounce selected words containing the two sounds.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to listen carefully and practise distinguishing between /ɔ/ and /ɔː/ in spoken words.

2. What sound is heard in “cot”?

topics.title: Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sounds /u/ and /uː/ Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 3 English Phonics
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (PHONICS)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 3
THEME - PHONEMIC AWARENESS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sounds /ɔ/ and /ɔ:/ Primary 3 (Basic 3) Week 2 English Studies
TOPIC - AURAL DISCRIMINATION OF THE SOUNDS /ʊ/ and /u:/
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction to phonemic awareness
2. Identification of the sounds /u/ and /uː/
3. Words containing /u/ and /uː/ Sounds
4. Pronunciation and listening practice
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the simple meaning of phonemic awareness.
2. Identify the sounds /u/ and /uː/ when they hear them.
3. Pronounce words containing the two sounds correctly.
4. Identify words containing /u/.
5. Identify words containing /uː/.
6. Distinguish between /u/ and /uː/ when listening.
7. Group words according to their vowel sounds.
8. Use selected words containing the sounds in simple sentences.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can listen to and identify common vowel sounds in simple words.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Word cards, Picture cards, Sound cards, Flashcards
2. Phonics chart
3. Writing board
4. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses listening, demonstration, repetition, pronunciation drills, questioning, word identification, comparison, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by saying familiar words containing the two sounds and asks pupils to listen carefully.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Phonics chart
5. Dictionary
6. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Phonemic awareness is the ability to hear and identify individual sounds in spoken words.
Today, pupils will listen carefully and distinguish between the sounds /u/ and /uː/.
The two sounds are similar, but they are different.
THE SOUND /u/
The sound /u/ can be heard in words such as:
- pull
- full
- foot
- good
- book
- look
- cook
- took
- put
- wood
Pupils listen to the teacher and repeat the words.
THE SOUND /uː/
The sound /uː/ can be heard in words such as:
- pool
- fool
- food
- moon
- soon
- room
- school
- cool
- boot
- spoon
Pupils listen to the teacher and repeat the words.
CONTRASTING WORD PAIRS
The following pairs help pupils hear the difference between /u/ and /uː/:
/u/: pull, full, foot, good, book, look, cook, took, put, wood
/uː/: pool, fool, food, moon, soon, room, school, cool, boot, spoon
The teacher pronounces each pair clearly. Pupils listen carefully and repeat.
AURAL DISCRIMINATION
Aural discrimination means listening carefully and identifying differences between sounds.
The teacher says one word at a time. Pupils listen and identify whether they hear /u/ or /uː/.
Examples:
- pull - /u/
- pool - /uː/
- full - /u/
- fool - /uː/
- foot - /u/
- food - /uː/
- good - /u/
- moon - /uː/
- look - /u/
- school - /uː/
LISTENING PRACTICE
The teacher says pairs of words. Pupils listen and say whether the vowel sounds are the same or different.
1. pull - pool → Different
2. full - fool → Different
3. foot - food → Different
4. good - moon → Different
5. book - look → Same
6. pool - school → Same
7. foot - good → Same
8. food - moon → Same
PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE
The teacher models the words clearly.
- /u/: pull, full, foot, good, book
- /uː/: pool, fool, food, moon, school
Pupils repeat the words individually and together.
SIMPLE SENTENCES
Please pull the door.
1. The cup is full.
2. My foot is clean.
3. The boy is good.
4. I have a book.
5. We swim in the pool.
6. Do not be a fool.
7. The food is ready.
8. The moon is bright.
9. I go to school every day.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Which sound is heard in “pull”? A. /u/ B. /uː/ C. /ɔ/
2. Which word contains the /uː/ sound? A. Full B. Fool C. Foot
3. Which word contains the /u/ sound? A. Pool B. Food C. Pull
4. Which pair has different vowel sounds?
A. pull - pool
B. book - look
C. pool - school
5. Which word contains the /uː/ sound? A. Foot B. Food C. Good
6. Which word contains the /u/ sound? A. Moon B. School C. Full
7. Which pair has the same vowel sound?
A. foot - good
B. foot - food
C. pull - pool
8. Which pair has different vowel sounds?
A. book - look
B. full - fool
C. food - moon
9. Which word contains the /uː/ sound? A. Look B. School C. Good
10. What should pupils do to distinguish between /u/ and /uː/?
A. Ignore the sounds
B. Guess the words
C. Listen carefully to the sounds
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. B
6. C 7. A 8. B 9. B 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that phonemic awareness means listening to and identifying individual sounds in spoken words.
They learned to distinguish between /u/ and /uː/ by listening to contrasting word pairs such as pull-pool, full-fool and foot-food.
Pupils also practised pronouncing the sounds, grouping words according to their vowel sounds and using selected words in simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher revises the previous lesson and says familiar words containing /u/ and /uː/. The teacher asks pupils to listen carefully.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify the sounds they hear.
Step 2: Introducing /u/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces /u/ and pronounces words such as pull, full, foot, good and book.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the sound and words.
Step 3: Introducing /uː/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces /uː/ and pronounces words such as pool, fool, food, moon and school.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the sound and words.
Step 4: Comparing the Sounds
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher presents contrasting pairs such as pull-pool, full-fool and foot-food and pronounces them clearly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify whether the vowel sounds are the same or different.
Step 5: Aural Discrimination Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher says individual words and asks pupils to identify whether they contain /u/ or /uː/.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and identify the sound they hear.
Step 6: Pronunciation Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher pronounces contrasting words and guides pupils to repeat them correctly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words individually and in groups.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five words containing /u/.
- Group 2: Identify five words containing /uː/.
- Group 3: Match contrasting pairs such as pull-pool, full-fool and foot-food.
- Group 4: Read selected words aloud and identify their vowel sounds.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, match, pronounce and present the words.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the sounds /u/ and /uː/ and the contrasting word pairs. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and pronounce selected words containing the two sounds.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to listen carefully to spoken words and practise distinguishing between /u/ and /uː/.
NEXT LESSON
Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sounds /ɔɪ/ and /eə/ Primary 4 (Basic 3) Week 4 English Studies
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is phonemic awareness?
2. What sound is heard in “pull”?
3. What sound is heard in “pool”?
4. Mention three words containing /u/.
5. Mention three words containing /uː/.

topics.title: Stories built on Dangers of Drug Abuse Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 3 English Structure
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (READING)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 3
THEME - STRUCTURE
PREVIOUS LESSON - Stories built on Road Safety Primary 3 (Basic 3) Week 1 and Week 2 English Structure
TOPIC - STORIES BUILT ON DANGERS OF DRUG ABUSE
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction to Drug Abuse
2. Reading a simple story
3. Using new words in simple sentences and Constructing simple sentences
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Read a simple story about the dangers of drug abuse.
2. Explain the simple meaning of drug abuse.
3. Identify new words in the story.
4. Give the meanings of selected new words.
5. Identify nouns and verbs in the story.
6. Use selected words in simple sentences.
7. State some dangers of drug abuse.
8. Construct simple sentences about avoiding drug abuse.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can read simple stories and identify common nouns and verbs.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
1. Story chart
2. Picture cards, Word cards, Flashcards
3. Drug-abuse prevention posters
4. Writing board
5. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses reading aloud, explanation, questioning, demonstration, repetition, sentence construction, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by showing pupils pictures about healthy and unhealthy choices and asks them what they can see.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Drug-abuse prevention materials
5. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Drug abuse means using drugs in a wrong or harmful way.
Some medicines are useful when they are used correctly and with proper guidance. However, using drugs without proper guidance or using harmful substances can cause serious problems.
Children should not take medicines or other drugs without proper guidance from a parent, caregiver, doctor, pharmacist or other qualified health professional.
STORY: TAIWO MAKES A WISE CHOICE
Taiwo was a primary school pupil. He liked playing football with his friends after school.
One day, an older boy offered Taiwo a substance and told him to try it. Taiwo knew that taking unknown substances could be harmful.
He remembered what his teacher had taught the class about drug abuse. He refused to take the substance and quickly told his mother about what had happened.
His mother praised him for making a wise choice. She explained that drug abuse can harm the body, affect learning and cause other serious problems.
Taiwo promised never to take unknown drugs or substances. He also encouraged his friends to make healthy choices.
UNDERSTANDING THE STORY
The story teaches pupils to:
- avoid unknown drugs and harmful substances;
- refuse drugs offered by other people;
- tell a trusted adult when someone offers them an unknown substance;
- use medicine only with proper guidance; and
- make healthy and safe choices.
NEW WORDS AND MEANINGS
1. Drug - a substance that can affect the body when taken.
2. Abuse - using something in a wrong or harmful way.
3. Substance - a type of material.
4. Harmful - able to cause harm.
5. Refuse - to say no to something.
6. Choice - something selected after thinking.
7. Healthy - good for the body and mind.
8. Trusted - believed to be safe and reliable.
9. Affect - to cause a change in something.
10. Avoid - to stay away from something.
SENTENCES FROM THE STORY
1. Taiwo was a primary school pupil.
2. He liked playing football.
3. An older boy offered him an unknown substance.
4. Taiwo refused to take it.
5. He told his mother what happened.
6. His mother praised him.
7. Drug abuse can harm the body.
8. Taiwo made a wise choice.
NOUNS IN THE STORY
A noun is the name of a person, place, animal or thing.
Examples from the story: Taiwo, Pupil, football, boy, substance, teacher, mother, body, friends
VERBS IN THE STORY
A verb is a word that shows an action.
Examples from the story: was, liked, playing, offered, try, knew, refused told, praised, explained, encouraged
MAKING SIMPLE SENTENCES
Pupils can use the new words to make simple sentences.
Examples:
1. I avoid harmful substances.
2. Taiwo made a good choice.
3. I refuse unknown drugs.
4. Drug abuse is harmful.
5. I tell a trusted adult.
6. We make healthy choices.
7. Drugs can affect the body.
8. We should avoid drug abuse.
DANGERS OF DRUG ABUSE
Drug abuse can:
1. harm the body;
2. affect learning;
3. cause poor behaviour;
4. make a person sick; and
5. lead to other serious problems.
6. Children should never use unknown drugs or substances.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Who was the main character in the story?
A. Taiwo
B. Kola
C. Musa
2. What did Taiwo like doing after school?
A. Swimming
B. Playing football
C. Cooking
3. What did the older boy offer Taiwo?
A. A book
B. A ball
C. An unknown substance
4. What did Taiwo do?
A. He took the substance.
B. He refused to take it.
C. He sold it.
5. Who did Taiwo tell about what happened?
A. His friend
B. His neighbour
C. His mother
6. What does “refuse” mean?
A. To say no
B. To run fast
C. To sleep
7. Which word is a noun?
A. Refuse
B. Harmful
C. Mother
8. Which word is a verb?
A. Football
B. Refused
C. Substance
9. Which sentence is correctly written?
A. Taiwo refused the unknown substance.
B. taiwo refused the unknown substance.
C. Taiwo refused the unknown substance.
10. Which is a danger of drug abuse?
A. Better learning
B. Harm to the body
C. Stronger eyesight
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. B 3. C 4. B 5. C
6. A 7. C 8. B 9. C 10. B
SUMMARY
Pupils read a story about Taiwo and learned about the dangers of drug abuse.
They learned new words such as drug, abuse, harmful, refuse, choice and avoid. They also identified nouns and verbs and practised using the new words in simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pictures of healthy and unhealthy choices and asks pupils what they can see.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and share what they know.
Step 2: Reading the Story
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher displays the story “Taiwo Makes a Wise Choice” and reads it aloud clearly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and read the story after the teacher.
Step 3: Understanding the Story
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains what happened in the story and asks pupils questions about Taiwo’s actions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and state what Taiwo did.
Step 4: New Words and Meanings
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces words such as drug, abuse, harmful, refuse, choice and avoid and explains their meanings.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words, repeat their meanings and give simple examples.
Step 5: Nouns and Verbs
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains nouns and verbs and guides pupils to identify them in the story.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify nouns and verbs and read them aloud.
Step 6: Making Simple Sentences
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates how to make simple sentences using words from the story.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils construct and read simple sentences.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five nouns from the story.
- Group 2: Identify five verbs from the story.
- Group 3: Give the meanings of five new words.
- Group 4: Make five simple sentences about avoiding drug abuse.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, explain, construct and present their answers.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the story, new words, nouns, verbs and dangers of drug abuse. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and state what they have learned about avoiding drug abuse.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to avoid unknown drugs and harmful substances and to tell a trusted adult if anyone offers them something they should not take.
NEXT LESSON
Stories Built on Good Health and Personal Hygiene | Primary 3 (Basic 3) Week 4 English Structure
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is drug abuse?
2. What did the older boy offer Taiwo?
3. What did Taiwo do?
4. Mention two dangers of drug abuse.
5. Make a sentence with the word “avoid.”

topics.title: Composition - Writing of Poem: Once I Saw A Little Bird Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 3 English Composition
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (COMPOSITION)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 3
THEME - STRUCTURE
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - ONCE I SAW A LITTLE BIRD
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Explain what a poem is.
3. Read a simple poem clearly.
4. Identify important words and ideas in a poem..
5. Copy and write the poem neatly.
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain what a poem is.
2. Read a simple poem clearly.
3. Identify important words and ideas in a poem.
4. Arrange simple sentences into lines of a poem.
5. Write a short poem about a little bird.
6. Use capital letters and full stops correctly.
7. Copy and write the poem neatly.
8. Create simple lines about a bird.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can write simple words and sentences and read short poems.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
1. Poem chart
2. Picture of a little bird
3. Word cards, Flashcards
4. Writing board
5. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses reading aloud, explanation, questioning, demonstration, repetition, guided writing, copying, sentence construction and group activities.
The teacher begins by showing a picture of a little bird and asking pupils simple questions about it.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Poetry book
5. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
A poem is a piece of writing arranged in short lines. Poems can be about people, animals, plants, nature and things we see around us.
A poem can use simple words and may have a rhythm or rhyme.
The teacher introduces a simple poem about a little bird.
SIMPLE POEM: ONCE I SAW A LITTLE BIRD
Once I saw a little bird,
Sitting on a tree.
It sang a happy song,
And flew away from me.
It had two little wings,
And feathers soft and bright.
It hopped upon the ground,
Then flew out of sight.
READING THE POEM
The teacher reads the poem aloud clearly.
Pupils listen carefully and read the poem after the teacher.
The teacher guides pupils to pronounce difficult words correctly.
NEW WORDS AND THEIR MEANINGS
1. Bird - an animal with feathers, wings and a beak.
2. Sitting - resting on a place.
3. Sang - made music with the voice.
4. Wings - parts of a bird used for flying.
5. Feathers - soft coverings on a bird’s body.
6. Bright - giving a lot of light or having a strong colour.
7. Hopped - moved by jumping.
8. Ground - the surface of the earth.
IMPORTANT IDEAS IN THE POEM
The poem tells us that:
- the child saw a little bird;
- the bird was sitting on a tree;
- the bird sang a happy song;
- the bird had two wings;
- the bird had soft and bright feathers;
- the bird hopped on the ground; and
- the bird eventually flew away.
WRITING A POEM
When writing a simple poem, pupils should:
- choose a simple topic;
- think about what they want to say;
- use short and clear sentences;
- arrange the sentences in lines;
- begin each line with a capital letter where appropriate;
- use punctuation correctly; and
- write neatly.
GUIDED WRITING
The teacher guides pupils to write a simple poem about a little bird.
Example:
My Little Bird
I saw a little bird,
It sat upon a tree.
It sang a lovely song,
Then flew away from me.
Pupils read the poem and copy it into their exercise books.
MAKING SIMPLE LINES ABOUT A BIRD
The teacher asks pupils questions to help them create lines.
Examples:
1. What did you see? - I saw a little bird.
2. Where was it? - It was on a tree.
3. What did it do? - It sang a song.
4. What did it use to fly? - It used its wings.
5. Where did it go? - It flew away.
6. Pupils can arrange these ideas into a short poem.
WRITING PRACTICE
Pupils write four simple lines about a little bird.
Example:
I saw a little bird.
It sat on a tree.
It sang a sweet song.
Then it flew away.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is a poem?
A. A shopping list
B. A piece of writing arranged in lines
C. A long number
2. What did the child see?
A. A tall man
B. A big dog
C. A little bird
3. Where was the bird sitting?
A. On a tree
B. In a car
C. In a house
4. What did the bird do?
A. It read a book.
B. It cooked food.
C. It sang a song.
5. What does a bird use to fly?
A. Hands
B. Wings
C. Shoes
6. What are feathers?
A. Coverings on a bird’s body
B. Parts of a tree
C. Pieces of paper
7. Which word means “moved by jumping”?
A. Hopped
B. Sang
C. Sat
8. Which sentence is correctly written?
A. i saw a bird.
B. I saw a bird.
C. I saw a bird
9. How should a poem be arranged?
A. In lines
B. In a shopping bag
C. In a box
10. Which of these is a good topic for a simple poem?
A. A difficult scientific theory
B. A broken machine with many parts
C. A little bird
ANSWER KEY
1. B 2. C 3. A 4. C 5. B
6. A 7. A 8. B 9. A 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that a poem is a piece of writing arranged in lines.
They read the poem “Once I Saw a Little Bird”, identified important ideas and learned new words such as bird, wings, feathers, bright and hopped.
Pupils also learned how to arrange simple ideas into lines and write a short poem.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows a picture of a little bird and asks pupils what they know about birds.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the picture and mention things they know about birds.
Step 2: Reading the Poem
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher displays the poem “Once I Saw a Little Bird” and reads it aloud clearly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and read the poem after the teacher.
Step 3: Understanding the Poem
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks simple questions about the bird, where it was and what it did.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and identify important ideas in the poem.
Step 4: New Words and Meanings
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces words such as bird, wings, feathers, bright and hopped and explains their meanings.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words, repeat their meanings and use some of them in simple sentences.
Step 5: How to Write a Poem
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a simple poem is written in short lines and demonstrates how to arrange simple sentences into lines.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration and arrange simple sentences into poem lines.
Step 6: Guided Writing
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher guides pupils to write four simple lines about a little bird.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils suggest ideas and write simple lines about the bird.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Read the poem aloud.
- Group 2: Identify five new words and give their meanings.
- Group 3: Identify five important ideas in the poem.
- Group 4: Write four simple lines about a little bird.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils read, identify words, discuss ideas, write poem lines and present their work.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning of a poem, the poem “Once I Saw a Little Bird,” new words and the steps for writing a simple poem. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and write four lines about a little bird.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to observe things around them and use simple words and ideas to write short poems.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is a poem?
2. What did the child see?
3. Where was the bird sitting?
4. Mention two things the bird did.
5. Write four simple lines about a little bird.

topics.title: Writing Composition About My Best Friend Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 4 English Writing
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (COMPOSITION)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 4
THEME - WRITING
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - MY BEST FRIEND
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction to composition writing
2. Meaning of a best friend and Talking about a best friend
3. Writing a simple composition
4. Guided and group writing
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain who a best friend is.
2. Mention the name of a best friend.
3. Describe a best friend using simple words.
4. State some things they do with their best friend.
5. Arrange ideas into simple sentences.
6. Write a short composition about a best friend.
7. Use capital letters and full stops correctly.
8. Write neatly and clearly.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can write simple sentences and describe familiar people.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
1. Composition chart
2. Picture of two friends
3. Word cards, Flashcards
4. Writing board
5. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses discussion, questioning, explanation, demonstration, sentence construction, guided writing, repetition and group activities.
The teacher begins by showing a picture of two friends and asks pupils simple questions about friendship.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Writing charts
5. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
A friend is someone we like, trust and enjoy spending time with.
A best friend is a very close friend. We can play, learn and share good times with our best friend.
When writing about a best friend, we can write about:
- the friend’s name;
- the friend’s age;
- where the friend lives;
- the friend’s appearance;
- the friend’s character;
- things we do together; and
- why we like the friend.
WORDS USED TO DESCRIBE A FRIEND
Some simple words we can use are:
- kind
- friendly
- helpful
- neat
- cheerful
- polite
- honest
- hardworking
- caring
- funny
GUIDED QUESTIONS
The teacher asks pupils questions to help them gather ideas.
1. What is your best friend’s name?
2. Is your best friend a boy or a girl?
3. How old is your best friend?
4. Where does your best friend live?
5. What does your best friend look like?
6. What kind of person is your best friend?
7. What do you do together?
8. Why do you like your best friend?
SIMPLE SENTENCES ABOUT A BEST FRIEND
Examples:
- My best friend’s name is Ada.
- She is seven years old.
- She lives near my house.
- She is kind and friendly.
- She helps me with my school work.
- We play together after school.
- We read storybooks together.
- I like her because she is caring.
SAMPLE COMPOSITION: MY BEST FRIEND
My Best Friend
My best friend’s name is Ada. She is seven years old. She is my classmate.
Ada is kind, friendly and helpful. She has short black hair and a lovely smile.
We sit together in class. We read and play together during break time. She also helps me when I need help.
I like Ada because she is a good friend. I am happy to have her as my best friend.
STEPS IN WRITING ABOUT MY BEST FRIEND
Pupils should follow these simple steps:
- Think about the friend they want to write about.
- Write the friend’s name.
- Write the friend’s age and other simple details.
- Describe the friend’s appearance.
- Describe the friend’s character.
- Write what they do together.
- Write why they like the friend.
- Check the work for capital letters, full stops and spelling.
WRITING PRACTICE
Pupils write a short composition of 5-8 sentences about their best friend.
They can use these questions as a guide:
- What is your friend’s name?
- How old is your friend?
- What does your friend look like?
- What kind of person is your friend?
- What do you do together?
- Why do you like your friend?
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Who is a best friend?
A. A very close friend
B. A stranger
C. A driver
2. Which word can describe a good friend?
A. Angry
B. Dirty
C. Kind
3. Which sentence is correctly written?
A. my best friend is Ada.
B. My best friend is Ada.
C. My best friend is ada.
4. What should you write first when describing your friend?
A. Your friend’s name
B. Your friend’s shoes only
C. Your friend’s food
5. Which of these can you do with a friend?
A. Break things
B. Fight all day
C. Play together
6. Complete the sentence: “My best friend is very ______.”
A. kind
B. table
C. school
7. Which sentence ends correctly?
A. My friend is helpful
B. My friend is helpful.
C. My friend is helpful,
8. Which word means “ready to help”?
A. Slow
B. Small
C. Helpful
9. A composition should contain ______.
A. sentences
B. only numbers
C. only pictures
10. Which is a good reason for liking a friend?
A. She breaks things.
B. She is kind and caring.
C. He fights everyone.
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. C 3. B 4. A 5. C
6. A 7. B 8. C 9. A 10. B
SUMMARY
Pupils learned how to write a simple composition about their best friend.
They learned how to introduce a friend, describe the friend’s appearance and character, state activities they do together and explain why they like the friend.
They also practised using capital letters, full stops and simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows a picture of two friends and asks pupils what they can see and what friends do together.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the picture and talk about friendship.
Step 2: Meaning of a Best Friend
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a best friend is a very close friend. The teacher gives simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and mention the names of their friends.
Step 3: Describing a Friend
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks questions about a friend’s name, age, appearance and character.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions about their best friends.
Step 4: Making Simple Sentences
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates how to turn the answers into simple sentences.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils make simple sentences about their best friends.
Step 5: Guided Composition
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher displays the sample composition “My Best Friend” and reads it aloud. The teacher explains how the ideas are arranged.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils read the composition and identify the information about the friend.
Step 6: Individual Writing
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher guides pupils to write 5-8 sentences about their best friend.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils write their compositions using the guided questions.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Mention five words that can describe a good friend.
- Group 2: Make five simple sentences about a friend.
- Group 3: Arrange five ideas in the correct order for writing about a friend.
- Group 4: Write a short composition of five sentences about a best friend.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, arrange sentences and present their work.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews how to write about a best friend and reminds pupils to use capital letters, full stops and correct spelling. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and read their compositions aloud.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to be kind, helpful, polite and caring towards their friends and to use simple sentences when writing about people they know.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. Who is a best friend?
2. Mention two words that can describe a good friend.
3. What is your best friend’s name?
4. Mention one thing you do with your best friend.
5. Write five sentences about your best friend.

topics.title: Pronunciation of Multi Syllabic Words Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 4 English English Studies
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (PHONICS)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 4
THEME - PHONICS
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - PRONUNCIATION OF MULTI SYLLABIC WORDS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of syllables
3. Meaning of multi-syllabic words and Identifying syllables in words
4. Breaking words into Syllables and Pronouncing multi-syllabic words
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain what a syllable is.
2. Explain what a multi-syllabic word is.
3. Identify syllables in simple words.
4. Divide multi-syllabic words into syllables.
5. Pronounce common multi-syllabic words correctly.
6. Listen and identify the number of syllables in words.
7. Use correct stress when pronouncing selected words.
8. Read multi-syllabic words clearly.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can pronounce simple one-syllable words and read simple sentences.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
1. Word cards, Flashcards, Picture cards
2. Word charts
3. Writing board
4. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses listening, demonstration, repetition, pronunciation drills, questioning, word identification, syllable clapping, comparison, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by saying familiar words and asks pupils to listen carefully to the number of beats or syllables they hear.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Pronunciation charts
5. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Words can be made up of one or more syllables.
A syllable is a part or beat of a word that we say together.
For example:
- cat - 1 syllable
- table - 2 syllables
- banana - 3 syllables
A multi-syllabic word is a word that has two or more syllables.
IDENTIFYING SYLLABLES
Pupils can clap their hands as they say a word to help them hear its syllables.
Examples:
- ta-ble - 2 syllables
- win-dow - 2 syllables
- ba-na-na - 3 syllables
- po-ta-to - 3 syllables
- to-ma-to - 3 syllables
- el-e-phant - 3 syllables
- um-brel-la - 3 syllables
- ed-u-ca-tion - 4 syllables
TWO-SYLLABLE WORDS
Examples:
- table - ta-ble
- teacher - teach-er
- window - win-dow
- garden - gar-den
- pencil - pen-cil
- mother - moth-er
- father - fath-er
- water - wa-ter
- market - mar-ket
- schoolbag - school-bag
The teacher pronounces each word clearly. Pupils listen and repeat.
THREE-SYLLABLE WORDS
Examples:
- banana - ba-na-na
- tomato - to-ma-to
- potato - po-ta-to
- elephant - el-e-phant
- umbrella - um-brel-la
- animal - an-i-mal
- family - fam-i-ly
- holiday - hol-i-day
- vegetable - veg-e-ta-ble
- beautiful - beau-ti-ful
Pupils clap once for each syllable as they pronounce the words.
FOUR-SYLLABLE WORDS
Examples:
- education - ed-u-ca-tion
- information - in-for-ma-tion
- examination - ex-am-i-na-tion
- celebration - cel-e-bra-tion
- communication - com-mu-ni-ca-tion
The teacher pronounces the words slowly and then at a normal speaking speed. Pupils listen and repeat.
HOW TO PRONOUNCE MULTI-SYLLABIC WORDS
Pupils should:
- listen carefully to the word;
- say the word slowly;
- divide the word into syllables;
- clap for each syllable;
- repeat the word several times;
- say the word at a normal speed; and
- listen for the stressed syllable.
WORDS FOR PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE
The teacher guides pupils to pronounce the following words:
Two syllables:
- table
- teacher
- window
- garden
- market
Three syllables:
- banana
- tomato
- potato
- elephant
- umbrella
Four syllables:
- education
- information
- examination
- celebration
- communication
STRESS IN MULTI-SYLLABIC WORDS
Some syllables are pronounced more strongly than others.
The teacher demonstrates the natural stress in selected words.
Examples:
- TA-ble
- TEACH-er
- ba-NA-na
- to-MA-to
- EL-e-phant
- um-BREL-la
Pupils listen and repeat the words.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is a syllable?
A. A paragraph
B. A sentence
C. A part or beat of a word
2. Which word has two syllables?
A. Cat
B. Table
C. Book
3. How many syllables are in “banana”?
A. One
B. Two
C. Three
4. Which word has three syllables?
A. Elephant
B. Chair
C. Ball
5. How many syllables are in “umbrella”?
A. Two
B. Three
C. Four
6. Which word has four syllables?
A. Education
B. Garden
C. Teacher
7. What can pupils do to help identify syllables?
A. Clap as they say the word
B. Close their books
C. Run around
8. Which word is divided correctly into syllables?
A. b-anana
B. ban-an-a
C. ba-na-na
9. Which word has three syllables?
A. School
B. Pencil
C. Tomato
10. What should pupils do when learning to pronounce a new multi-syllabic word?
A. Listen and repeat
B. Guess the word
C. Ignore the sounds
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. B
6. A 7. A 8. B 9. C 10. A
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that a syllable is a part or beat of a word.
They learned that multi-syllabic words have two or more syllables. Pupils practised breaking words into syllables, clapping for each syllable and pronouncing words such as table, banana, elephant, umbrella and education.
They also learned to listen for the stressed syllable when pronouncing multi-syllabic words.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher says simple words and asks pupils to listen to the number of beats they hear.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen, repeat the words and clap the beats they hear.
Step 2: Meaning of Syllables
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a syllable is a part or beat of a word and gives simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the examples.
Step 3: Identifying Syllables
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher displays words such as table, banana and elephant and demonstrates how to count their syllables.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils say the words and clap once for each syllable.
Step 4: Two- and Three-Syllable Words
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces two- and three-syllable words and divides them into syllables.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words and divide them into syllables.
Step 5: Four-Syllable Words
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces words such as education, information and celebration and demonstrates their pronunciation.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and repeat the words.
Step 6: Stress and Pronunciation Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates how some syllables are stressed more strongly than others and guides pupils to pronounce selected words correctly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen, repeat the words and practise the stressed syllables.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five two-syllable words.
- Group 2: Identify five three-syllable words.
- Group 3: Divide five multi-syllabic words into syllables.
- Group 4: Pronounce five multi-syllabic words aloud.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, divide, pronounce and present the words.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning of syllables, multi-syllabic words, syllable division and pronunciation. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and pronounce selected multi-syllabic words.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to listen carefully, divide words into syllables and practise pronouncing multi-syllabic words clearly.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is a syllable?
2. What is a multi-syllabic word?
3. How many syllables are in “banana”?
4. Divide “elephant” into syllables.
5. Pronounce “umbrella” correctly.

topics.title: Phonic Pronunciation of Diphthong: Vowel Sounds /ai/ and /ei/ Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 5 English Phonics
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (PHONICS)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 5
THEME - PHONEMIC AWARENESS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Phonemic Awareness: Aural Discrimination of the Sounds /ɔɪ/ and /eə/ Primary 4 (Basic 3) Week 4 English Studies
TOPIC - VOWEL SOUNDS /ai/ and /ei/
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction to diphthongs
2. Identification of the sounds /aɪ/ and /eɪ/
3. Words containing /aɪ/ and /eɪ/
4. Guided pronunciation practice
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the simple meaning of a diphthong.
2. Identify the sounds /aɪ/ and /eɪ/.
3. Pronounce words containing /aɪ/ correctly.
4. Pronounce words containing /eɪ/ correctly.
5. Distinguish between /aɪ/ and /eɪ/.
6. Identify words containing the two sounds.
7. Group words according to their vowel sounds.
8. Use selected words containing the sounds in simple sentences.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can listen to and pronounce familiar vowel sounds in simple words.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Word cards, Picture cards, Sound cards, Flashcards
2. Phonics chart
3. Writing board
4. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses listening, demonstration, repetition, pronunciation drills, questioning, word identification, comparison, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by saying familiar words containing the two sounds and asks pupils to listen carefully.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Phonics chart
5. Dictionary
6. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
A diphthong is a vowel sound that begins with one sound and moves to another sound within the same syllable.
In this lesson, pupils will learn to pronounce the diphthong sounds /aɪ/ and /eɪ/.
Examples:
- /aɪ/ - as in my, five, light
- /eɪ/ - as in day, name, rain
THE SOUND /aɪ/
The sound /aɪ/ is heard in words such as:
- my
- fly
- five
- bike
- kite
- light
- night
- right
- time
- smile
Pupils listen to the teacher and repeat the words.
THE SOUND /eɪ/
The sound /eɪ/ is heard in words such as:
- day
- say
- play
- name
- game
- rain
- train
- cake
- make
- late
Pupils listen to the teacher and repeat the words.
COMPARING /aɪ/ AND /eɪ/
The two sounds are different.
- /aɪ/: my, five, bike, kite, light
- /eɪ/: day, name, game, rain, cake
The teacher pronounces the words clearly. Pupils listen and repeat.
WORD IDENTIFICATION
The teacher says words and pupils identify whether the word contains /aɪ/ or /eɪ/.
Examples:
- my - /aɪ/
- day - /eɪ/
- five - /aɪ/
- name - /eɪ/
- bike - /aɪ/
- game - /eɪ/
- light - /aɪ/
- rain - /eɪ/
- kite - /aɪ/
- cake - /eɪ/
PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE
The teacher models the sounds and words clearly.
- /aɪ/: my, five, bike, kite, light, night
- /eɪ/: day, name, game, rain, cake, train
Pupils repeat the words individually and together.
LISTENING AND PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE
The teacher says a word. Pupils listen and raise the /aɪ/ sound card or /eɪ/ sound card according to the sound they hear.
Examples:
- fly → /aɪ/
- play → /eɪ/
- time → /aɪ/
- late → /eɪ/
- smile → /aɪ/
- train → /eɪ/
- night → /aɪ/
- make → /eɪ/
SIMPLE SENTENCES
- This is my book.
- I can fly a kite.
- I have five pencils.
- The bike is new.
- The light is on.
- Today is a sunny day.
- Please say your name.
- We play together.
- The rain is falling.
- I like this cake.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Which sound is heard in “five”? A. /aɪ/ B. /eɪ/ C. /uː/
2. Which word contains the /eɪ/ sound? A. Kite B. Day C. Light
3. Which word contains the /aɪ/ sound? A. Name B. Rain C. Bike
4. Which word contains the /eɪ/ sound? A. Game B. Night C. Fly
5. Which word contains the /aɪ/ sound? A. Cake B. Five C. Train
6. Which pair contains the same vowel sound?
A. bike - kite
B. bike - cake
C. day - night
7. Which pair contains different vowel sounds?
A. my - fly
B. rain - train
C. light - late
8. Which word contains the /eɪ/ sound?
A. Smile
B. Make
C. Time
9. Which word contains the /aɪ/ sound?
A. Play
B. Name
C. Night
10. What is a diphthong?
A. A sound that moves from one vowel sound to another
B. A word with two consonants
C. A word with two syllables
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. B
6. A 7. C 8. B 9. C 10. A
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that a diphthong is a vowel sound that moves from one sound to another within the same syllable.
They learned to pronounce and identify the sounds /aɪ/ and /eɪ/ using words such as five, bike, kite, light, day, name, game, rain and cake.
Pupils also practised identifying the two sounds and using selected words in simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher revises the previous lesson and says familiar words containing /aɪ/ and /eɪ/. The teacher asks pupils to listen carefully.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify the sounds they hear.
Step 2: Introducing /aɪ/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces /aɪ/ and pronounces words such as my, five, bike, kite and light.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the sound and words.
Step 3: Introducing /eɪ/
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher introduces /eɪ/ and pronounces words such as day, name, game, rain and cake.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the sound and words.
Step 4: Comparing the Sounds
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher presents words containing /aɪ/ and /eɪ/ and pronounces them clearly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify the sound in each word.
Step 5: Word Identification
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher says individual words and asks pupils to identify whether they contain /aɪ/ or /eɪ/.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and identify the sound they hear.
Step 6: Pronunciation Practice
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher pronounces words containing the two sounds and guides pupils to repeat them correctly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils pronounce the words individually and in groups.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Identify five words containing /aɪ/.
- Group 2: Identify five words containing /eɪ/.
- Group 3: Sort word cards according to /aɪ/ and /eɪ/.
- Group 4: Read selected words aloud and identify their vowel sounds.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify, sort, pronounce and present the words.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning of a diphthong, the sounds /aɪ/ and /eɪ/, and examples of words containing the sounds. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and pronounce selected words containing the two sounds.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to listen carefully and practise pronouncing words containing the diphthong sounds /aɪ/ and /eɪ/.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils:
1. What is a diphthong?
2. What sound is heard in “five”?
3. What sound is heard in “day”?
5. Mention three words containing /aɪ/.
6. Mention three words containing /eɪ/.

topics.title: Types of Sentences Primary 3 (Basic 3) First Term Week 5 English Structure
topics.content:
ENGLISH STUDIES (STRUCTURE)
PRIMARY 3 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 5
THEME - STRUCTURE
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - TYPES OF SENTENCES
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of a sentence
3. Identifying types of sentences
4. Constructing simple sentences
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of a sentence.
2. Identify different types of sentences.
3. Recognise a statement, question, command and exclamation.
4. Use the correct punctuation marks.
5. Construct simple sentences of different types.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can read and write simple sentences.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
1. Sentence cards, Flashcards, Picture cards
2. Sentence charts
3. Writing board
4. Exercise books and pencils
METHOD OF TEACHING
The teacher uses explanation, demonstration, questioning, sentence identification, repetition, comparison, guided practice and group activities.
The teacher begins by saying different simple sentences and asks pupils to listen and identify what each sentence does.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. English Studies textbook
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Sentence charts
5. Relevant teaching materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.
Examples:
- The boy is running.
- I like mangoes.
- She is my friend.
There are different types of sentences. Each type has a different purpose.
The four common types of sentences are:
1. Statement
2. Question
3. Command
4. Exclamation
1. STATEMENT
A statement tells us something or gives information.
A statement usually ends with a full stop (.)
Examples:
- I am a pupil.
- The sun is hot.
- My mother is cooking.
- We go to school every day.
- The dog is under the table.
2. QUESTION
A question asks something.
A question ends with a question mark (?)
Examples:
- What is your name?
- Where do you live?
- Are you a pupil?
- Do you like rice?
- Who is your teacher?
3. COMMAND
A command tells someone to do something. It can also give an instruction.
A command usually ends with a full stop (.)
Examples:
- Sit down.
- Open your book.
- Close the door.
- Wash your hands.
- Come here.
A command may also end with an exclamation mark (!) when it is given strongly.
Example: Stop!
4. EXCLAMATION
An exclamation expresses strong feeling such as joy, surprise, fear or excitement.
An exclamation ends with an exclamation mark (!)
Examples:
- What a beautiful flower!
- Hurray! We won the game!
- Oh no! I lost my pencil!
- What a big elephant!
- Wow! That is wonderful!
IDENTIFYING TYPES OF SENTENCES
Pupils should look at what each sentence does.
- I have a new bag. Statement
- Where is your book? Question
- Open the door. Command
- What a lovely dress! Exclamation
PUNCTUATION MARKS
Different sentences use different punctuation marks.
- Statement - .
- Question - ?
- Command - .
- Exclamation - !
Examples:
- Statement: The girl is happy.
- Question: Is the girl happy?
- Command: Come here.
- Exclamation: What a happy girl!
COMPARING THE TYPES OF SENTENCES
The same idea can be expressed in different ways.
1. Statement: The baby is sleeping.
2. Question: Is the baby sleeping?
3. Command: Let the baby sleep.
4. Exclamation: What a lovely baby!
The purpose of each sentence helps us identify its type.
CONSTRUCTING SIMPLE SENTENCES
Pupils should construct simple sentences of each type.
Examples:
- Statement: My father is a teacher.
- Question: Is your father a teacher?
- Command: Read your book.
- Exclamation: What a beautiful house!
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is a sentence?
A. A group of words expressing a complete thought
B. A single letter
C. A number
2. Which type of sentence gives information?
A. Question
B. Statement
C. Exclamation
3. Which punctuation mark ends a question?
A. .
B. !
C. ?
4. Which sentence is a question?
A. I am happy.
B. Where is your bag?
C. Close the door.
5. Which sentence is a command?
A. Open your book.
B. Where is your book?
C. What a big book!
6. Which sentence is an exclamation?
A. The boy is running.
B. Is the boy running?
C. Wow! That is beautiful!
7. Which punctuation mark usually ends a statement?
A. Full stop
B. Question mark
C. Exclamation mark
8. “Wash your hands.” is a ______.
A. question
B. command
C. statement
9. “What is your name?” is a ______.
A. question
B. command
C. exclamation
10. “Hurray! We won the game!” is a ______.
A. statement
B. question
C. exclamation
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. B 3. C 4. B 5. A
6. C 7. A 8. B 9. A 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that a sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.
They learned four common types of sentences: statement, question, command and exclamation.
They also learned the punctuation marks used with each type and practised constructing simple sentences.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher writes simple sentences on the board and reads them aloud. The teacher asks pupils what each sentence does.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils read the sentences and say what each sentence tells or asks.
Step 2: Statement
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a statement gives information and demonstrates examples ending with full stops.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify statements and read them aloud.
Step 3: Question
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a question asks something and demonstrates examples ending with question marks.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify questions and practise asking simple questions.
Step 4: Command
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a command gives an instruction and demonstrates simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify commands and give simple instructions to one another.
Step 5: Exclamation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that an exclamation expresses strong feelings and demonstrates examples ending with exclamation marks.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify exclamations and read them with appropriate expression.
Step 6: Identifying Sentence Types
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher displays different sentences and guides pupils to identify their types and punctuation marks.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the types of sentences and state the punctuation marks used.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Write five statements.
- Group 2: Write five questions.
- Group 3: Write five commands.
- Group 4: Write five exclamations.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, read and present their sentences.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the four types of sentences and their punctuation marks. The teacher gives pupils the assessment questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and identify the types of selected sentences.
CONCLUSION
The teacher encourages pupils to identify the purpose of a sentence and use the correct punctuation mark when writing statements, questions, commands and exclamations.

Teacher asks pupils:

2. Mention four types of sentences.
3. What is a statement?
4. What punctuation mark is used at the end of a question?
5. Give one example of a command.

By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:

4. Write a short composition about a dog.
5. Arrange ideas in a simple and meaningful order.
